definition: A chip company that designs semiconductors but pays a foundry such as TSMC to manufacture them; NVIDIA has been fabless since its founding.
A way of drawing 3D shapes from curved patches described by second-order equations, used by NVIDIA's first chip (NV1) instead of the flat triangles the industry standardised on.
Microsoft's 3D graphics programming interface for Windows (part of DirectX); it standardised on triangles, which made chips built around other primitives incompatible with most games.
The steps that position each 3D vertex on screen and compute how light falls on it; GeForce 256 (1999) moved them from the CPU into graphics hardware.
An early graphics-chip design in which each rendering stage is hard-wired circuitry with a few settings, rather than a processor that runs programs.
A small program that a GPU runs once per vertex or per pixel; once shaders became programmable (GeForce 3, 2001) the GPU became a general parallel processor, the precursor to CUDA.
A single chip that integrates CPU cores, graphics, memory controllers and other functions, as used in phones and tablets (for example NVIDIA's Tegra).
The chip (or block) that handles a phone's cellular radio protocols; NVIDIA bought Icera in 2011 to supply one and wound the business down in 2015.
